ask.ch1-u1-dilutionchain-5.foreverdilute: No, and working out why is the interesting part. Each step keeps one part in ten, so after twenty steps you would have one part in a hundred billion billion. Somewhere before that you run out of particles entirely: the last one either goes into the beaker you kept or the one you poured away. The colour does not fade to nothing, it stops because there is nothing left to fade.
Could I dilute it forever and always see some colour?
ask.ch1-u1-dissolvebox-3.levelrise.a: It rises for most things. Salt is unusual because its particles are small enough to slip into gaps that already exist. Drop in a marble and the level jumps, because a marble cannot fit between water particles. The lesson is not that dissolving never raises the level, it is that there is space in there at all.
ask.ch1-u1-dissolvebox-3.levelrise.q: So does the water level never rise at all, no matter what I add?
ask.ch1-u1-dissolvebox-3.saltlimit.a: Nothing about the gaps, but there is a limit, and you can find it with a spoon. Keep adding and eventually the salt sits at the bottom and will not go in however long you stir. The water is then saturated: the gaps are taken. Warm the water and a little more goes in, because the particles spread out and make room. You will meet this properly as solubility in the next chapter.
ask.ch1-u1-dissolvebox-3.saltlimit.q: If the salt just fills the gaps, what stops me adding salt forever?
ask.ch1-u2-diffusionrace-3.whyslow.a: Because they do not travel in a straight line. A particle moves very fast but collides billions of times a second and is knocked sideways each time, so it staggers rather than travels. Crossing a beaker takes hours even though each step is fast. Smell reaches you quickly through air because gas particles are much further apart and collide far less.
ask.ch1-u2-diffusionrace-3.whyslow.q: If particles move that fast, why does ink take hours instead of a second?
ask.ch1-u3-bondbreaker-4.whynotclump.a: Because attraction is not the only thing happening. Particles are also moving, and the hotter they are the harder they pull away. A solid is what you get when attraction is winning. A gas is what you get when movement is winning. Heating something is a way of changing which side wins, which is exactly what the next unit is about.
ask.ch1-u3-bondbreaker-4.whynotclump.q: If every particle attracts every other, why is anything not one big lump?
ask.ch1-u4-syringetest-2.squashtonothing: No. You can squeeze the space out, but not the particles: they take up room themselves and will not pass through one another. Push hard enough and they are forced so close that attraction takes hold and the gas turns into a liquid, which is how the gas in a cooking cylinder is stored.
If a gas is mostly empty space, can I squash it down to nothing?
ask.ch1-u5-heatingcurve-2.getitback.a: It comes straight back. Put the water in a freezer and it gives up exactly the same amount of energy as it turns back into ice. Nothing was lost, it was stored in pulling the particles apart. This is also why ice cools a drink so well: it takes that energy out of the drink to melt.
ask.ch1-u5-heatingcurve-2.getitback.q: The energy vanished into melting. Is it gone for good?
ask.ch1-u5-heatingcurve-2.hotterflame.a: No, it gets shorter. A bigger flame delivers energy faster, so the ice melts sooner, but the temperature still will not move until the last of it has gone. You cannot heat ice above its melting point while it is still ice. That is why the flat part is worth trusting: it is not about how fast you heat, it is about where the energy is going.
ask.ch1-u5-heatingcurve-2.hotterflame.q: What if I use a much bigger flame? Does the flat part go away?
Because pressure alone is not always enough. Every gas has a temperature above which no amount of squeezing will liquefy it: the particles are simply moving too fast for attraction to take hold. Room temperature is well above that point for nitrogen and oxygen. Cool the air far enough first and then pressure works, which is exactly how liquid oxygen is made for hospitals.
There is pressure on the air in this room, so why is it not liquid?
Only until the surroundings catch up. As the water cools it starts drawing heat from whatever it touches, and it settles where the two balance. That is exactly why a matka keeps water cool but never freezes it, and why sweating cools you without turning you to ice.
If the fastest particles keep leaving, does the water get colder and colder?
ask.ch1-u7-evaporationlab-2.whynotallgon: Because particles go both ways. Some leave the water and some come back out of the air, and once those two rates match, the level stops changing even though evaporation never stops. That balance is what humidity measures. In a closed bottle it happens quickly. Over an ocean, rain is the returning half.
If water evaporates at any temperature, why has the sea not dried up?
ask.ch1-u8-challenge-1.humidsweat.a: Because sweat only cools you when it evaporates, and on a humid day the air is already close to full. The sweat sits on your skin instead of leaving it, so you get all the wetness and none of the cooling. It is the same reason a desert cooler works beautifully in a dry April and disappoints during the monsoon.
ask.ch1-u8-challenge-1.humidsweat.q: If sweating cools me down, why do I feel worse on a humid day when I sweat more?
ch1.a1.steps:
1. Fill a 100 mL beaker halfway with water.
2. Mark the water level on the glass.
3. Add a spoon of salt and stir with a glass rod until it disappears.
4. Look at your mark again.
ch1.a1.watchFor: The salt vanishes from sight. Does the water level move? Taste a drop. Is the salt still there?
ch1.a11.steps:
1. Take three 100 mL syringes and seal the nozzles with rubber corks.
2. Pull out all three pistons. Leave the first empty, fill the second with water, and the third with pieces of chalk.
3. Smear a little vaseline on each piston and push them back in.
4. Now try to push each piston further in.
ch1.a11.watchFor: Which piston moves easily, which barely moves at all, and what does that tell you about the space between the particles inside?
ch1.a12: Heating ice, all the way to steam
ch1.a12.steps:
1. Put about 150 g of ice in a beaker.
2. Clamp a thermometer so the bulb touches the ice, not the glass.
3. Heat on a low flame. Write down the temperature every 30 seconds.
4. Note the temperature when the ice starts to melt, and when the last of it has gone.
5. Keep heating and stirring until the water boils, and keep recording.
ch1.a12.watchFor: Watch the thermometer while ice and water are both in the beaker. The flame is still on. Is the reading climbing?
ch1.a13.steps:
1. Crush some camphor into a china dish.
2. Put an inverted funnel over the dish.
3. Plug the funnel stem with cotton.
4. Heat slowly and watch the inside of the funnel.
ch1.a13.watchFor: Look for liquid camphor in the dish. There is none. Solid went straight to vapour, and vapour went straight back to solid on the cool glass.
ch1.a14.steps:
1. Put 5 mL of water in a test tube and stand it near a window or under a fan.
2. Put 5 mL in an open china dish next to it.
3. Put 5 mL in another open china dish, but inside a cupboard.
4. Write down the room temperature.
5. Record how long each one takes to dry, and repeat the whole thing on a rainy day.
ch1.a14.watchFor: The water never boiled, and it still disappeared. Which dish went first, and what was different about it?
ch1.a2.steps:
1. Dissolve 2 or 3 crystals of potassium permanganate in 100 mL of water.
2. Take 10 mL of that solution and add it to 90 mL of clean water.
3. Take 10 mL of the new solution and add it to another 90 mL of clean water.
4. Keep going, 5 to 8 times.
ch1.a2.watchFor: The colour gets fainter each time. Does it ever disappear completely? Try the same thing with 2 mL of Dettol and use your nose instead of your eyes.
ch1.a3.steps:
1. Put an unlit incense stick in a corner of the room. Walk towards it. How close must you get to smell it?
2. Now light it.
3. Sit back down in your usual place. Wait.
ch1.a3.watchFor: Nobody fanned the smoke towards you. How did the smell cross the room on its own?
ch1.a4.steps:
1. Fill two beakers with water.
2. Let one drop of ink slide down the inside wall of the first beaker.
3. Let one drop of honey slide down the inside wall of the second.
4. Do not stir. Leave both somewhere they will not be disturbed.
5. Look again after an hour, then after a day.
ch1.a4.watchFor: Which one spreads? How long does the ink take to colour the whole beaker with nobody touching it?
ch1.a5: Hot and cold, side by side
ch1.a5.steps:
1. Fill one glass with hot water and another with cold.
2. Drop one crystal of copper sulphate into each. Let it settle at the bottom.
3. Do not stir either glass.
4. Watch the water just above each crystal, and keep watching.
ch1.a6.steps:
Go outside. Split the class into four groups.
1. Group 1 links arms tightly, the way Idu-Mishmi dancers do.
2. Group 2 holds hands.
3. Group 3 touches fingertips only.
4. Group 4 runs at the other three and tries to break each chain into as many pieces as possible.
ch1.a6.watchFor: Which chain broke first, and which held longest? If each student is a particle, which group is the solid, which the liquid, and which the gas?
ch1.a7.steps:
1. Take an iron nail, a piece of chalk and a rubber band.
2. Try to break each one by hammering, cutting or stretching.
3. Rank them from easiest to hardest to break.
ch1.a8.steps:
1. Take a container of water.
2. Try to cut the surface with your finger.
3. Lift your finger out and look at the surface.
ch1.groupActivity.steps:
1. Put some chickpeas or dry peas in a transparent jar.
2. Sew a string to the centre of a large rubber sheet or cut-open balloon and tape it so it holds.
3. Stretch the rubber sheet over the mouth of the jar and tie it on.
4. Run your fingers up and down the string, first slowly, then hard.
ch1.groupActivity.watchFor: Slow tugging gives you a solid, a little more gives you a liquid, and vigorous shaking gives you a gas. You are supplying the energy that heat normally supplies.
ch1.item.airInBalloon.why: Gas. It has mass, it exerts pressure on the walls, and it fills the balloon completely.
ch1.item.chalkPowder.why: Solid, for the same reason as sugar. A powder pours, but each grain keeps its own shape.
ch1.item.cookingOil.why: Flows, fixed volume, takes the shape of the container.
ch1.item.honey.why: Liquid. It flows very slowly, but it does flow, and it takes the shape of its jar.
ch1.item.iceCube.why: Solid water. Same substance as the liquid, different arrangement of particles.
ch1.item.lpg: The gas in a cooking cylinder
ch1.item.lpg.why: It is stored as a liquid under pressure, but it burns as a gas and fills any space it is released into.
ch1.item.milk.why: Fixed volume, but it takes the shape of whatever you pour it into.
ch1.item.pen.why: Fixed shape, fixed volume, will not compress.
ch1.item.rubberBand.why: Solid. It changes shape when you pull it and springs back when you let go. Pull hard enough and it breaks rather than flows.
ch1.item.sponge.why: Solid. You are not compressing the sponge, you are squeezing trapped air out of its holes.
ch1.item.steam.why: Water in the gaseous state. It spreads to fill whatever room it is in.
ch1.item.sugar.why: Solid. The heap takes the shape of the jar, but look at one crystal: its own shape never changes.
ch1.u1.check.a: One crystal contains an enormous number of extremely small particles
ch1.u1.check.a.fb: Right. To spread through a thousand litres and still be visible, one crystal must hold a colossal number of particles, each far too small to see.
ch1.u1.check.b: The colour spreads into the air gaps inside the water
ch1.u1.check.b.fb: There is no air in those gaps. The spaces between water particles are empty. If they held air, the water would fizz when you warmed it. What fills them is the dissolved particles themselves.
ch1.u1.check.c: The crystal breaks down and turns into water
ch1.u1.check.c.fb: Nothing was destroyed or converted. Boil the water away and the potassium permanganate is still there, back as a solid. Dissolving spreads a substance out. It does not unmake it.
ch1.u1.check.prompt: Two or three crystals of potassium permanganate can colour about a thousand litres of water. What does that tell you?
ch1.u1.dilution.caption: Each step keeps one part in ten. After eight steps you are down to one part in a hundred million, and you can still see it.
ch1.u1.dissolve.caption: Add the salt, then zoom in. Watch where the salt particles actually go.
ch1.u1.goal: Show that matter is made of separate particles with gaps between them, and that those particles are unimaginably small.
ch1.u1.intro: Ancient Indian thinkers said everything was built from five basic elements, the Panch Tatva: air, earth, fire, sky and water. Greek thinkers reached almost the same list. They were wrong about the five, but right about the big idea, that a small number of building blocks make everything you can see. This chapter finds the real building blocks.
ch1.u1.observe.explanation: The salt particles did not push the water aside. They dropped into gaps that were already there, between the water particles. That is only possible if water is not a solid block of stuff, but a crowd of separate particles with space between them.
ch1.u1.observe.prompt: The level barely moved. Where did the salt fit?
ch1.u1.predict.prompt: You dissolve a full spoon of salt in the water. What happens to the water level?
ch1.u1.predict.rise: It rises, because you added something
ch1.u1.title: Everything is made of particles
ch1.u1.zoom.caption: This scale will follow you through the whole book. Right now you have two stops on it. By Chapter 4 you will have eight.
ch1.u2.check.a: Hot food gives its particles more energy, so they travel further and faster through the air
ch1.u2.check.a.fb: Exactly. Higher temperature means higher kinetic energy, faster diffusion, and a smell that reaches across the room.
ch1.u2.check.b: Hot air currents carry the smell, and without them nothing would move
ch1.u2.check.b.fb: Currents help, but they are not the cause. In Activity 1.4 the ink spread through still water in a beaker with no currents at all. Particles move on their own.
ch1.u2.check.c: Cold food has particles that have stopped moving
ch1.u2.check.c.fb: Particles never stop. Cold food still smells, you just have to get closer. Cooling slows particles down, and it never brings them to a halt.
ch1.u2.check.prompt: You can smell hot sizzling food from several metres away, but you have to lean right over cold food to smell it. Why?
ch1.u2.diffusion.caption: No stirring allowed. Drop a crystal in each and watch the graph build itself.
ch1.u2.goal: Show that particles move on their own without being stirred, and that heating makes them move faster.
ch1.u2.observe.explanation: The particles are moving by themselves, all the time, in every direction. This is why they slowly mix without help, and the mixing is called diffusion. Heating gives every particle more energy, so it moves faster, so the hot glass mixes sooner. That energy of motion has a name: kinetic energy.
ch1.u2.observe.prompt: Nobody stirred anything, and the colour still spread. What is pushing it?
ch1.u2.predict.neither: Neither spreads, because nothing is stirring them
ch1.u2.predict.prompt: Two glasses, one hot water and one cold. Drop an identical crystal in each and do not stir either. What happens?
ch1.u2.predict.same: Both spread at the same rate
ch1.u2.title: Particles never stop moving
ch1.u3.bonds.caption: Pull the chain apart. The human chain from the game is drawn underneath, doing the same thing.
ch1.u3.check.a.fb: Correct. Oxygen is a gas and its particles barely hold on at all, water is a liquid, and sugar is a solid with the strongest grip of the three.
ch1.u3.check.b: Sugar, then water, then oxygen, because solids are heavier
ch1.u3.check.b.fb: That is the right list, backwards. The question asked for increasing force, so the weakest comes first. Also, weight is not the point here. The force of attraction is.
ch1.u3.check.c: They are all the same, because oxygen has no particles to attract
ch1.u3.check.c.fb: Oxygen has particles and they do have mass. Weigh an empty balloon, fill it, weigh it again. A gas is matter. Its particles simply hold on to each other very weakly.
ch1.u3.check.prompt: Put water, sugar and oxygen in increasing order of force of attraction between their particles.
ch1.u3.goal: Show that particles attract each other, and that the strength of that attraction is what makes one material harder to break than another.
ch1.u3.observe.explanation: Every substance has a force of attraction holding its particles together, but the strength of that force is different for every substance. Chalk gives up easily, iron does not. The same idea explains why you can push a finger through water but not through wood, and why the water surface closes up again behind your finger.
ch1.u3.observe.prompt: All three are solids, and yet they needed very different amounts of force. Why?
ch1.u3.predict.prompt: Which needs the most force before its particles come apart?
ch1.u3.title: Particles hold on to each other
ch1.u4.check.a: Its particles move fast in all directions and constantly strike the walls
ch1.u4.check.a.fb: Right. Pressure is the total force of those collisions spread over each unit of area. More collisions, or faster ones, means more pressure.
ch1.u4.check.b: Gas is weightless and floats upwards against the top of the container
ch1.u4.check.b.fb: Gas is not weightless. Weigh a balloon before and after filling it and you will see the difference. And the pressure pushes on every wall, including the bottom, not just the top.
ch1.u4.check.c: The air trapped between the gas particles expands
ch1.u4.check.c.fb: There is nothing between the gas particles. The space is empty. The gas particles themselves are what strike the walls.
ch1.u4.check.prompt: Why does a gas push outwards on the walls of its container?
ch1.u4.goal: Explain shape, volume, compressibility and rigidity for all three states using spacing and attraction between particles.
ch1.u4.observe.explanation: Compressing something means pushing its particles closer together. In a gas there is a huge amount of empty space, so there is somewhere for them to go. In a solid the particles are already touching, so there is nowhere left. This is why an entire cylinder of LPG fits in your kitchen, and why a gas cylinder is worth transporting.
ch1.u4.observe.prompt: The air compressed easily and the chalk hardly moved. What is different inside them?
ch1.u4.particlebox.caption: One slider, three states. Watch the property panel change as you heat and cool.
ch1.u4.predict.equal: All three move about the same
ch1.u4.predict.prompt: Which syringe will let you push the piston in furthest?
ch1.u4.sort.prompt: Sort these into solid, liquid and gas. Some of them are deliberately awkward.
ch1.u4.syringe.caption: Push each piston and watch the particle view. On a phone you will feel the difference too.
ch1.u4.title: Solid, liquid, gas
ch1.u5.calc1.prompt: Convert 293 K to the Celsius scale.
ch1.u5.calc1.step1: To go from kelvin to Celsius, subtract 273.
ch1.u5.calc1.trap: Adding 273 instead of subtracting. Kelvin numbers are always the larger ones, so going to Celsius must make the number smaller.
ch1.u5.calc2.prompt: Convert 373 degrees Celsius to the kelvin scale.
ch1.u5.calc2.step1: To go from Celsius to kelvin, add 273.
ch1.u5.calc2.trap: Reading 373 as the boiling point of water and answering 373 K. That is 373 degrees Celsius, which is far hotter. Read the unit before you calculate.
ch1.u5.check1.a: The ice must absorb its latent heat of fusion from the drink before it can melt
ch1.u5.check1.a.fb: Exactly. Both start at the same temperature, but the ice pulls a large extra amount of energy out of the drink just to become water. Water at 273 K takes nothing extra.
ch1.u5.check1.b: Ice is colder than water at the same temperature
ch1.u5.check1.b.fb: They are at the same temperature, 273 K. That is what the question says. The difference is not temperature, it is the energy the ice absorbs while melting without its temperature changing at all.
ch1.u5.check1.c: The ice particles melt and disappear, taking heat with them
ch1.u5.check1.c.fb: The particles do not melt and nothing disappears. The ice particles become the water particles. What changes is how they are arranged, not the particles themselves.
ch1.u5.check1.prompt: Why does ice at 273 K cool a drink better than water at 273 K?
ch1.u5.check2.a: Steam, because it releases its latent heat of vaporisation onto your skin as it condenses
ch1.u5.check2.a.fb: Correct. Steam first dumps a large amount of hidden energy as it turns back to water on your skin, and only then does it start to cool. Boiling water only cools.
ch1.u5.check2.b: Boiling water, because liquid carries more heat than gas
ch1.u5.check2.b.fb: Both are at 373 K, so the temperature is identical. Steam carries the extra latent heat of vaporisation on top, which is released the instant it touches you.
ch1.u5.check2.prompt: What burns you more severely, boiling water at 373 K or steam at 373 K?
ch1.u5.goal: Explain why temperature stays flat during a change of state, and what latent heat is doing.
ch1.u5.heating.caption: Hold the flame on and watch both sides. The graph draws itself. Tap a flat stretch when you see one.
ch1.u5.latentHeat: The energy needed to turn 1 kg of a solid into liquid at its melting point is the latent heat of fusion. The energy needed to turn 1 kg of a liquid into gas at its boiling point is the latent heat of vaporisation. This is why water at 0 degrees Celsius holds more energy than ice at 0 degrees Celsius, even though a thermometer cannot tell them apart.
ch1.u5.observe.explanation: Look at the particle view during a flat stretch. The particles are not speeding up, they are breaking free of each other. All the energy going in is being spent on pulling particles apart, not on making them move faster, and temperature only measures how fast they move. The moment the last particle breaks free, the temperature starts climbing again. This hidden energy is called latent heat, and latent means hidden.
ch1.u5.observe.prompt: You never took the flame away, and the temperature stopped climbing twice. Where did that energy go?
ch1.u5.predict.falls: Falling, because the ice is cooling the water
ch1.u5.predict.flat: Staying at one reading and not moving
ch1.u5.predict.prompt: The flame is on. There is ice and water in the beaker together. What is the thermometer doing?
ch1.u5.predict.rises: Rising steadily, because heat is still going in
ch1.u5.sublimation.caption: No liquid stage at any point. Solid to gas is sublimation, gas to solid is deposition.
ch1.u5.title: Melting, boiling and hidden heat
ch1.u6.check.a: Cool it a long way down and compress it hard at the same time
ch1.u6.check.a.fb: Right. Cooling removes the energy that keeps particles apart and pressure pushes them together. Industrial gas plants do exactly this.
ch1.u6.check.b: You cannot. Oxygen is a gas and has no liquid form
ch1.u6.check.b.fb: Every gas has a liquid form under the right conditions. Liquid oxygen is real, and hospitals keep it in tanks. A gas is a state, not a permanent identity.
ch1.u6.check.c: Pump the air out so the oxygen particles have nothing to bounce off
ch1.u6.check.c.fb: Lowering the pressure does the opposite of what you want. It gives the particles more room and keeps them gaseous. You need to force them together, not give them space.
ch1.u6.check.prompt: How would you turn the oxygen in this room into a liquid?
ch1.u6.dryIce: Solid carbon dioxide is stored under high pressure. Drop it to normal atmospheric pressure and it goes straight from solid to gas without ever becoming a liquid, which is why it is called dry ice. It is the only common solid you can hold that leaves nothing wet behind.
ch1.u6.goal: Show that pressure, not just temperature, decides which state a substance is in.
ch1.u6.label.caption: Six arrows, six names. This is Exercise 9 from your textbook.
ch1.u6.observe.explanation: Temperature and pressure together decide the state. Raising pressure forces particles closer until attraction takes over and a gas becomes a liquid. This is why LPG sits as a liquid in your kitchen cylinder and becomes a gas the moment you open the valve and drop the pressure.
ch1.u6.observe.prompt: You found three regions on the map. What are the two things that decide which one you are in?
ch1.u6.phase.caption: Wander around. The map behind you fills in as you discover each region.
ch1.u6.predict.no: No, only cooling can liquefy a gas
ch1.u6.predict.onlyCooling: Only if you cool it at the same time
ch1.u6.predict.prompt: Can you turn a gas into a liquid without cooling it at all, just by squeezing?
ch1.u6.predict.yes: Yes, enough pressure alone can do it
ch1.u6.title: Squeezing a gas into a liquid
ch1.u7.challenge.brief: You have wet clothes and 45 minutes. Set the conditions to get them dry in time.
ch1.u7.challenge.debrief: Spread wide, warm, windy and dry. That is why washing goes on a line outdoors on a sunny day and not in a bucket in a damp corner.
ch1.u7.check.a: Dry air can still absorb water vapour, so evaporation is fast and takes more heat away
ch1.u7.check.a.fb: Right. Humidity is how much water vapour the air is already carrying. Once the air is nearly full, evaporation slows down and the cooling stops working.
ch1.u7.check.b: Dry air is colder to begin with
ch1.u7.check.b.fb: A hot dry day is not colder than a hot humid day. The cooling does not come from the air being cold, it comes from water evaporating and carrying energy away.
ch1.u7.check.c: The water inside gets hot enough to boil
ch1.u7.check.c.fb: Nothing boils in a desert cooler. Evaporation happens at every temperature, and that is the whole point of this unit.
ch1.u7.check.prompt: Why does a desert cooler work better on a hot dry day than on a humid one?
ch1.u7.cooling.caption: Escaping particles are highlighted. Keep an eye on the average energy reading as they leave.
ch1.u7.evap.caption: Four sliders. Change one at a time and find out which ones actually matter.
ch1.u7.goal: Explain evaporation below boiling point, what speeds it up, and why it cools the surface it leaves.
ch1.u7.observe.explanation: At any temperature, some particles happen to be moving faster than others. A few of the fastest ones, right at the surface, have enough energy to escape into the air. That is evaporation, and it needs no boiling. Because it only happens at the surface, spreading the water out speeds it up. This is why you spread clothes out on a line instead of leaving them in a heap.
ch1.u7.observe.prompt: The water never reached 100 degrees Celsius and it still dried up completely. How?
ch1.u7.observe2.explanation: It lowered it. If the fastest members of a crowd keep leaving, the average speed of who is left goes down, and lower average speed means lower temperature. The escaping particles take that energy from whatever they are touching, which is your palm. Nothing cold came in. Energy went out.
ch1.u7.observe2.prompt: Only the fastest particles left. What did that do to the average energy of the ones that stayed?
ch1.u7.predict.all: Temperature, surface area and wind, and low humidity as well
ch1.u7.predict.prompt: Which of these actually makes water evaporate faster?
ch1.u7.predict2.coldAir: Cold air rushes in to replace the liquid
ch1.u7.predict2.fastLeave: The escaping particles carry energy away from your palm
ch1.u7.predict2.prompt: Pour a little acetone on your palm. It feels cold. Why?
ch1.u7.predict2.waterCold: The acetone was already cold when you poured it
ch1.u7.title: Why a puddle dries and why sweat cools you
ch1.u8.challenge.brief: One room, a village in Karnataka, a hot dry afternoon in April, and no electricity at all. Keep the drinking water cool and make the room bearable. Pick your interventions and justify each one by naming the mechanism it uses.
ch1.u8.challenge.debrief: Every one of these works by evaporation. The matka sweats through its own porous walls and the escaping water takes heat with it. A wet curtain cools the air passing through it. Water on the roof carries away heat as it dries. Cotton clothes soak up sweat and spread it out for evaporation, which is exactly the surface area effect from Activity 1.14. People worked all this out centuries before anyone wrote down the word latent heat.
ch1.u8.goal: Use everything from the chapter to solve a real problem with no electricity.
ch1.u8.title: Chapter challenge: the summer problem
ch1.u8.zoom.caption: Two stops down, six to go. Chapter 2 adds three of them.
gloss.atmospheric-pressure: The push of the air around us on everything it touches.
gloss.beaker: A glass cup with a lip, used for holding and heating liquids in a laboratory.
gloss.boiling-point: The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout, not just at the surface.
gloss.camphor: A white solid with a strong smell, used in worship and as a moth repellent.
gloss.compressible: Able to be squashed into a smaller space. Gases are, solids are not.
gloss.condense: When a gas cools and turns back into a liquid. It is why droplets form on a cold glass.
gloss.crystal: A solid whose particles are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern.
gloss.density: How much mass is packed into a given space.
gloss.deposition: When a gas turns straight into a solid without becoming a liquid first.
gloss.diffusion: When two substances mix into each other on their own, without anyone stirring them.
gloss.dissolve: When a solid spreads right through a liquid until you cannot see it any more. It is still there.
gloss.evaporation: When a liquid turns into a gas at its surface, at any temperature, without boiling.
gloss.fluid: Something that flows and takes the shape of its container. Liquids and gases are fluids.
gloss.funnel: A cone with a tube at the bottom, for pouring into a narrow opening.
gloss.fusion: Another word for melting: a solid changing into a liquid.
gloss.humidity: How much water vapour the air is already holding. Damp air makes things dry more slowly.
gloss.kelvin: A temperature scale used in science. 0 degrees Celsius is 273 kelvin.
gloss.kinetic-energy: The energy something has because it is moving. Hotter particles have more of it.
gloss.latent-heat: Hidden heat. Energy that goes into changing a state instead of raising the temperature, which is why the thermometer stops moving while ice melts.
gloss.mass: How much matter something contains. Measured in kilograms.
gloss.matka: An earthen pot for water. Its clay walls let a little water seep through and evaporate, which keeps the rest cool.
gloss.matter: Anything that takes up space and has mass. Everything around you is matter.
gloss.melting-point: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
gloss.particle: One of the tiny pieces that all matter is made of. Far too small to see.
gloss.pressure: How hard something pushes on each unit of area.
gloss.rigid: Stiff. Keeps its shape instead of flowing or bending.
gloss.solute: The substance that dissolves, such as the salt in salt water.
gloss.solvent: The substance that does the dissolving, usually the one there is more of. Water is the most common one.
gloss.sublimation: When a solid turns straight into a gas without becoming a liquid first. Camphor does this.
gloss.syringe: A tube with a plunger, used to push or draw in liquid or air.
gloss.vapour: A substance in its gas form, especially one that is usually a liquid. Steam is water vapour.
gloss.volume: How much space something takes up.
mis.coolingIsColdComingIn.correction: Nothing cold arrives. The fastest particles leave and take their energy with them, lowering the average energy of what remains.
mis.coolingIsColdComingIn.statement: Evaporation cools a surface because cold air moves in.
mis.dissolvingDestroys.correction: It is only spread out. Boil the water away and the solid comes back unchanged.
mis.dissolvingDestroys.statement: When something dissolves it is destroyed or turns into the liquid.
mis.evaporationOnlyAtBoiling.correction: Evaporation happens at every temperature, from the surface, whenever a fast particle escapes.
mis.evaporationOnlyAtBoiling.statement: A liquid only becomes vapour at its boiling point.
mis.gapsContainAir.correction: They are empty. If those gaps held air, dissolved salt would have nowhere to go and the water level would rise.
mis.gapsContainAir.statement: The spaces between particles are filled with air.
mis.gasesHaveNoMass.correction: Weigh a balloon empty and then full. A gas is matter, it has mass, and it exerts pressure.
mis.mixingNeedsStirring.correction: Particles move by themselves, so an ink drop colours a whole still beaker with nobody touching it.
mis.mixingNeedsStirring.statement: Two substances only mix if something stirs them.
mis.particlesThemselvesMelt.correction: The particles are identical before and after. Only their arrangement and freedom of movement change.
mis.particlesThemselvesMelt.statement: When ice melts, the particles themselves melt or change.
mis.solidParticlesStatic.correction: They vibrate constantly about fixed positions. Cooling slows particles down and never stops them.
mis.solidParticlesStatic.statement: Particles in a solid do not move at all.
mis.temperatureRisesWhileMelting.correct: It holds flat until the last of the solid is gone, because the energy is breaking particles apart rather than speeding them up.
mis.temperatureRisesWhileMelting.stateme: Temperature keeps climbing while a solid melts.
path.guided.blurb: Every artifact in the order it was designed to be met. Follow it start to finish, or ignore it and pick whatever looks interesting.
path.guided.title: The full route
ask.ch1-u2-do-4.streaks.q: In the hot glass the colour shot upwards in streaks instead of spreading evenly. Is that still diffusion?
ask.ch1-u2-do-4.streaks.a:
Mostly, no, and noticing the streaks is the sharpest thing you can do in this activity.

Water that has been warmed at the bottom of the glass is slightly lighter than the water above it, so it rises, and it carries the colour up with it in exactly those plumes and swirls you saw. That is the water itself moving, carrying the colour as a passenger. It has its own name, convection, and it is not the same thing as diffusion.

Diffusion is the slow part. It is what you saw in the ink and honey beaker, which needed an hour before anything was obvious and a day before the colour reached everywhere. Heating really does make diffusion faster, because every particle moves quicker, but only a few times faster, nowhere near fast enough to cross a glass in a minute. The swirls simply got there first.

This is worth more than the activity it came from. When you measure something, something else can quietly be doing the work, and your result looks like an answer when it is really a different question. That is why the ink beaker has to sit somewhere nobody will knock it: stopping the water from moving is the only way to watch the particles move on their own.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: I dissolved the salt and the water level barely moved. Where did the salt go?
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: Into the gaps between the water particles. The particles were never packed solid, so the salt fits between them instead of adding to the height.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: "It melted" or "it became water". Both mean the salt has stopped existing, which is the idea this whole unit exists to undo. Ask them to taste it, or to say what would be left if you boiled the water away.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: After eight dilutions the colour has nearly gone. Has the potassium permanganate run out?
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: No. It is spread so thin that too few particles reach the eye to look coloured. They are all still there, just far apart.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: "It divided into smaller and smaller pieces." The textbook's own wording invites this. Particles spread out; they do not split.
recap.s.u1.q3.ask: Give me a number for how small a particle is.
recap.s.u1.q3.answer: Every honest answer is a comparison rather than a number: millions of them in a crystal you can barely see.
recap.s.u1.q3.listenFor: A confident number. Someone guessing "about a millimetre" has not had the scale land yet, and the dilution is the evidence to go back to.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Why can you smell perfume from several metres away with nobody fanning it?
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: Its particles are moving on their own and spread through the air until some reach your nose.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: "The air carried it" or "the wind". Partly right, and worth taking seriously: in perfectly still air it would still arrive, just far more slowly.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: The hot glass coloured faster than the cold one. What did the heat actually change?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: It gave every particle more energy, so they move faster and mix sooner.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: "Heat pushed the colour upwards." Listen for anyone describing streaks or swirls: they have spotted convection, which is a sharper observation than the answer you were fishing for.
recap.s.u2.q3.ask: Ink took an hour to cross the beaker. Particles move hundreds of metres a second. Why so slow?
recap.s.u2.q3.answer: They collide billions of times a second and get knocked sideways, so they stagger rather than travel.
recap.s.u2.q3.listenFor: Silence, or "the ink is heavy". This is the question that separates having memorised the definition from having understood it.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Put these in increasing order of force between particles: water, sugar, oxygen.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Ordering by how heavy or how common they are. Ask what state each is in at room temperature: gas, liquid, solid, and the order falls out of that.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: You snapped the chalk and stretched the rubber band. What does the difference tell you?
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: The force holding particles together is not the same in every substance.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: "Chalk is weak." Careful: chalk is brittle, not weakly held. Diamond is the hardest thing in the room and it also shatters.
recap.s.u3.q3.ask: Easier to cut with a knife: water or an iron nail? What does that say about the particles?
recap.s.u3.q3.answer: Water, because its particles hold on to each other far more loosely than iron's do.
recap.s.u3.q3.listenFor: Laughter at the idea of cutting water. Push them: your hand goes through it, so something is genuinely weaker.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: What is the physical state of water at 25 degrees, at 0 degrees, and at 100 degrees?
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Liquid at 25. At 0 and at 100 it can be either, because those are exactly the melting and boiling points and both states sit together there.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: "Ice at 0, steam at 100", said quickly and confidently. The entire point of the question is that those two temperatures are the change itself, not one side of it.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: Give me two reasons an iron almirah counts as a solid.
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: It keeps its shape with no container, and it barely compresses however hard you push.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: "Because it is hard." Hardness is not one of the defining properties. Shape and compressibility are.
recap.s.u4.q3.ask: You pushed all three syringes. Which one moved, and why that one?
recap.s.u4.q3.answer: Only the air. Its particles have large gaps to be squeezed into; in the water and the solid they are already touching.
recap.s.u4.q3.listenFor: "Gas is lighter." Weight has nothing to do with it. Spacing does.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: Why does ice at 273 K cool a drink better than water at 273 K?
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: The ice has to absorb its latent heat of fusion before it can melt, and it takes that heat from the drink.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: "Ice is colder." They are at the same temperature, which is precisely what makes the question worth asking. Say the two numbers aloud and let them sit.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: Which gives the worse burn, boiling water or steam? Why?
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Steam, because it carries the latent heat of vaporisation on top of already being at 100 degrees.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: "Steam, because it is hotter." The right answer for the wrong reason. Ask what temperature steam is.
recap.s.u5.q3.ask: The flame stayed on but the thermometer stopped rising. Where was the energy going?
recap.s.u5.q3.answer: Into pulling the particles apart against their attraction. The thermometer cannot see that, because it only measures motion.
recap.s.u5.q3.listenFor: "The thermometer broke" or "the heat escaped". Try banning the word heat as a noun for this question: make them say what the energy is doing rather than where the heat is.
recap.s.u5.q4.listenFor: Adding instead of subtracting. Worth one quick check that the direction is secure before moving on.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: Name all six changes of state.
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: Melting, freezing, vaporisation, condensation, sublimation and deposition.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Four confident answers and two blanks. Sublimation and deposition are the ones that go missing, because they skip the state everyone pictures.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: The LPG cylinder in your kitchen. Is what is inside it a gas or a liquid?
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: Mostly liquid, held that way by pressure. It turns to gas on the way out.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: "Gas, it is called cooking gas." The name is the trap, and it is a good one. Ask why the cylinder is so heavy.
recap.s.u6.q3.ask: Naphthalene balls vanish over weeks and leave nothing behind. What happened?
recap.s.u6.q3.answer: They sublimed: solid straight to gas, with no liquid stage at all.
recap.s.u6.q3.listenFor: "They melted and then evaporated." Ask whether anyone has ever seen a puddle under the cupboard. If not, it did not happen.
recap.s.u7.q1.ask: Water boils at 100 degrees. So why does a puddle dry up at 30?
recap.s.u7.q1.answer: Evaporation happens at any temperature, from the surface, because some particles always have enough energy to escape. Boiling is the whole liquid changing at once.
recap.s.u7.q1.listenFor: "The sun boiled it away." Boiling and evaporation collapsing into one idea is the misconception here, and it is extremely common.
recap.s.u7.q2.ask: Why does sweating cool you, when the sweat starts at your own body temperature?
recap.s.u7.q2.answer: The fastest particles escape first, so the ones left behind are slower, which is what cooler means, and they draw heat from your skin.
recap.s.u7.q2.listenFor: "Because it feels wet" or "because of the breeze". Ask why a wet arm still cools in perfectly still air.
recap.s.u7.q3.ask: Name two things you would change to dry the washing faster, and say why each works.
recap.s.u7.q3.answer: Spread it out, for more surface area, and put it in the wind, which carries the escaped particles away. Warmer and drier air count too.
recap.s.u7.q3.listenFor: "Put it in the sun" only. True, but it is one factor out of four, and the other three are the ones they can control indoors.
recap.s.u8.q1.ask: Explain how a matka keeps water cool. Use the word particle at least once.
recap.s.u8.q1.answer: Water seeps through the pores and evaporates off the outside. The fastest particles leave and take energy with them, pulling heat out of the water still inside.
recap.s.u8.q1.listenFor: "The mud is cold" or "clay is naturally cooling". The material is not doing the cooling, the evaporation is. A glazed pot proves it: seal the pores and it stops working.
recap.s.u8.q2.ask: Would a matka still work in a room where the air is already full of water vapour?
recap.s.u8.q2.answer: Barely. If the air cannot take up more water, evaporation nearly stops, and the cooling stops with it.
recap.s.u8.q2.listenFor: "Yes, because it is still mud." A good test of whether the mechanism landed or just the example.
recap.s.u8.q3.ask: On a humid coastal day, which cools you better: a desert cooler or a plain fan?
recap.s.u8.q3.answer: The fan. A desert cooler works by evaporation, and humid air will not accept much more water.
recap.s.u8.q3.listenFor: "The cooler, it is bigger." Ask what the cooler is actually doing to the air.
aid.s.u7.meaning: To move away fast, which is what the water is doing.
aid.s.u7.D.note: The drier the air, the faster it takes more water. On a humid day the washing stays wet.
aid.s.u7.A.note: Wind carries away the escaped particles, so the air just above stays hungry for more.
aid.s.u7.S.note: Spread it out and more particles sit at the surface, where escaping happens.
aid.s.u7.H.note: Warmer particles move faster, so more of them have enough energy to break free.
zoom.hand.label: Your own hand
zoom.hand.blurb: Where everybody starts. You can see it without help.
zoom.grain.label: A grain of sand
zoom.grain.blurb: Still visible, just. A hundred of them across your palm.
zoom.glass.label: What a magnifying glass shows
zoom.glass.blurb: Ten times smaller again. The edge of what an eye can do.
zoom.drop.label: Inside a drop of water
zoom.drop.blurb: Past the eye entirely. A microscope's world begins here.
zoom.particle.label: A single particle of matter
zoom.particle.blurb: A hundred thousand times smaller than the drop. Nobody has ever seen one directly.
